title: View of the Roman Forum
creator: Giovanni Battista Piranesi
depictedPeriod: Rome in the eighteenth century, including ancient ruins
rightsStatement: Public-domain object; the Met Open Access API marks object 363433 isPublicDomain=true. Open Access images released under CC0.
requiredAttribution: Giovanni Battista Piranesi / The Metropolitan Museum of Art, Harris Brisbane Dick Fund, 1937. 37.45.3(58).
altText: An etched view across the Roman Forum, with small figures among ancient columns, arches and later buildings.
caption: Piranesi, Roman Forum, ca. 1775. A later view of the Roman world’s remains.
historicalFit: An eighteenth-century view, not an eyewitness image of ancient Rome. Pliny wrote the letters shown here from Bithynia, not this location.
editorialReason: Give the Witnesses collection a visual sense of records surviving alongside ruins.

title: Saint Augustine
creator: Philippe de Champaigne
sourceInstitution: Los Angeles County Museum of Art
license: Public domain (underlying painting and faithful two-dimensional reproduction in the United States)
rightsStatement: Champaigne died in 1674. Faithful reproduction of a public-domain two-dimensional painting; PD-Art basis, not an institutional CC0 grant. LACMA credits its photograph © Museum Associates/LACMA. The equivalent Commons file separately documents the painting as PD-Art. No claim that LACMA waived its stated photographic credit.
requiredAttribution: Philippe de Champaigne, Saint Augustine, circa 1645. Gift of The Ahmanson Foundation, LACMA. Photo: Museum Associates/LACMA.
altText: Augustine writes with a quill while looking toward the word VERITAS; he holds a flaming heart in his other hand.
caption: Champaigne’s Augustine, circa 1645. A writer pictured with a burning heart.
historicalFit: Later devotional art, not a portrait from Augustine’s lifetime. The heart and light are the painter’s imagery.
editorialReason: Let readers compare Augustine’s opening address with the symbols a later painter chose for him.

title: Saint Perpetua and her child
creator: Mosaic artist: unknown. Photograph: Enric.
depictedPeriod: Later devotional representation of Perpetua and her son
sourceInstitution: Montserrat Abbey; photograph via the Perpetua and Felicitas Exhibit
rightsStatement: Exact exhibit record and linked Wikimedia file identify Enric’s photograph as CC BY-SA 3.0. Local derivative resized and converted to WebP; full composition retained. Derivative distributed under the same license.
requiredAttribution: Enric / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0. Via Perpetua and Felicitas Exhibit. Resized and converted to WebP.
altText: A mosaic shows a haloed Perpetua holding a small child against her body, their hands touching.
caption: Perpetua and her child, Montserrat. Devotional mosaic; artist and date unknown.
historicalFit: Later devotional art. It does not establish the appearance of Perpetua, her son or the prison.
editorialReason: Compare the lasting image of mother and child together with an account that narrates their separation.

title: Mother’s Kiss
creator: Mary Cassatt
rightsStatement: Object page explicitly identifies this media as public domain. NGA Open Access policy releases these images under CC0. Verified 2026-11-04.
requiredAttribution: Mary Cassatt, Mother’s Kiss, 1890–1891. Rosenwald Collection, 1943.3.2759. Courtesy National Gallery of Art, Washington.
altText: A mother bends to kiss a small child held against her body, in a color print by Mary Cassatt.
caption: Mary Cassatt, Mother’s Kiss, 1890–1891. An artistic parallel, not a portrayal of Perpetua.
historicalFit: A nineteenth-century artwork placed beside an ancient account as an artistic comparison. Neither a historical likeness nor evidence of the prison or its occupants.
editorialReason: Let the physical closeness of mother and child precede the account of separation. The whole artwork remains available; a reading screen covers the composition after refusal, without altering the figures.
